summary: Johann Heinrich Kalthoff worked in Indology and other fields. He studied at Münster, Bonn (Ph.D. 1829), and under Silvestre de Sacy and Abel-Rémusat. He served as Privatdozent at Münster (1830–1839) and taught French at Gymnasium Paulinum (1831).
Johann II Bernoulli studied at the University of Basel (~1723–1729) and later held an academic post there (~1743–1790).

Johann III Bernoulli was a scholar in Indology, history, archaeology, and other fields. Educated at Neuchâtel and Basel (doctorate under Johann II and Daniel Bernoulli), he directed the Berlin Observatory (1767) and the Prussian Academy of Sciences (1791).
Philosopher Johann Jakob Engel studied at the University of Rostock (~1757–1762) and the University of Leipzig (~1762–1765). He also taught Wilhelm von Humboldt.

Indologist Johann Jakob Meyer studied at Concordia Senior College, Concordia Seminary, and the University of Chicago under Carl Darling Buck (Ph.D. 1900). He served as a docent at the University of Chicago from 1908 to 1919.

Johann Kirste worked in Indology and linguistics. He studied at Graz, Leipzig, Berlin, Jena, Vienna (Ph.D.), and Paris, training with Georg Bühler. He held posts at the University of Vienna and the University of Graz, becoming ordinary professor in 1902.

Johann Peter Rottler, a scholar in Indology and linguistics, studied at the University of Strasbourg. He served with the Danish-Halle Mission (~1776–1817), directed the Tranquebar Botanical Garden, and worked at the Female Orphan Asylum and Vepery Mission.

Johann Philipp Fabricius worked in linguistics and Indology. He studied law at the University of Giessen (~1728–1732) and theology at the University of Halle-Wittenberg (~1732–1739), later succeeding Benjamin Schultze in 1742.

Johann Reinhold Forster studied at the Joachimsthalsches Gymnasium and the University of Halle-Wittenberg (1753–1765). In 1780, he was appointed Professor of Natural History at the University of Halle-Wittenberg.

Religious studies scholar Johann Tobias Beck studied at the University of Tübingen (~1822–1826). He later held academic posts at the University of Basel (~1836–1843) and the University of Tübingen (~1843–1878).

Johann Wilhelm Andreas Pfaff, working in Indology and other fields, studied at the University of Tübingen (~1790–1795). He held posts at the University of Tartu (~1803–1809), University of Würzburg (~1815–1817), and University of Erlangen-Nuremberg (~1818–1835).

Van Lohuizen-de Leeuw specialized in Indology and archaeology. Educated at Leiden and Utrecht (Ph.D. under Jan Gonda), she taught at Cambridge (1951–1959) and directed the Institute of South Asian Archaeology at the University of Amsterdam (1958–1983).

Johanna Narten specialized in linguistics, Iranian and Central Asian studies, and Indology. She studied at Saarland University and the University of Erlangen-Nuremberg, earning her PhD under Karl Hoffmann and habilitation, later serving there as Assistentin (1973–1977).

Johannes Baunack, an Indology and linguistics scholar, earned his Ph.D. at the University of Leipzig under Georg Curtius, also studying under Friedrich Zarncke, Hermann Brockhaus, and Adalbert Kuhn. He subsequently taught at the Alte Nikolaischule from 1878 to 1900.

Johannes Beltz works in Indology, religious studies, and Buddhist studies. He studied at Halle-Wittenberg, Lausanne, and EPHE (PhD under Marie-Louise Reiniche and Johannes Bronkhorst). He held posts at Heidelberg University (1996–2001) and Museum Rietberg (from 2001).

Johannes Bronkhorst specializes in Indology, Buddhist studies, and philosophy. He studied at VU Amsterdam, Rajasthan, Pune (PhD under S. D. Joshi), and Leiden. He held posts at the Kern Institute and served as professor at the University of Lausanne (1987–2011).
Johannes Brune, a scholar of Indology and linguistics, studied at Kiel University from 1903 to 1909, where he earned his Ph.D. His teachers included Hermann Oldenberg and Paul Deussen.

Johannes Edvard Lehmann, a scholar of religion and Iranian studies, studied at Copenhagen and Leiden. He taught at Copenhagen (1896–1910), was Professor of Theology at Berlin (1910–1913), and served as Professor of Religion at Lund (1913–1928).

Johannes Friedrich worked in linguistics, history, and archaeology. He studied at the University of Leipzig (~1911–1916) and later held posts at Leipzig (~1924–1950) and the Free University of Berlin (~1950–1961).

Indologist and archaeologist Johannes Gijsbertus de Casparis studied at Leiden University (~1934–1939). He later held posts at SOAS University of London (~1957–1981) and served as professor at Leiden University from 1978 to 1986.
